scenes.narration: Every minute, more than {claim:cited.market.youtube_500h_per_min} of new video go up on YouTube. Most of it only works if you can see it, and hear it.
{claim:cited.gbd.blind_2020} people are blind. They need to hear what is on screen.
Erika Wolf, writing for the American Council of the Blind, remembers leaving shows not having any inkling of what really took place.
{claim:cited.who.hearing_430m} live with disabling hearing loss. They need captions that also say what sounds.
{claim:cited.oecd.piaac_lit_level1_oecd_avg} of adults read at the lowest levels. They need simpler words, at a slower pace. And many people need the video in their own language.

Doing this by hand takes about {claim:cited.market.maa_20_hours} of work for one hour of TV, and costs {claim:cited.price.3play_industry_range_low} to {claim:cited.price.3play_industry_range_high} a minute. So most video never gets it.
He said: this is Hubble's famous photograph. But if you can't see the screen, you never find out what it shows.
There was no pause in his speech, so AccessCast held the picture while the description was read. Gemma 4, running on AMD, wrote every word, and code checked it.

This is AccessCast. One video, made for every viewer: for people who can't see the screen, people who can't hear, people who want simpler words, and for people who speak Hindi, Italian, Spanish, French or Portuguese.
On our site, every viewer picks what they need, and the same video plays for them.
If you can't see the screen, a voice describes what happens, in the pauses.
If you can't hear, captions show what is said, and the sounds.
If reading is hard, the same lines, in simpler words.
And in Hindi, Italian, Spanish, French and Portuguese, each with its own voice. Listen.
How does it work? Whisper listens. Gemma 4 31B, on AMD, looks at the frames and writes. Code checks every line, and Gemma repairs what fails. A person approves. Then every version is made.
Here is that NASA clip, step by step. Whisper writes down every word, and pins each one to the moment it is said.
The code measures the pauses between the words. This clip is mostly talk, so there are only a few.
Gemma looks at still frames from each scene, and lists only what it can see.
From that list alone, Gemma writes one line, inside a word budget: a man in a NASA polo shirt speaks to the camera.
Code checks it, and stops it. A blind viewer can already hear him speak, so it wastes the pause. The model never decides whether its own line is good enough.
The line goes back to Gemma with the exact rule it broke. The new line: he looks at the camera. The code checks again, and it passes.
Reviewers work in our review app by keyboard alone, with the frames, the checks and every repair in front of them.
Anyone can drop in their own video, and watch every step run.
This is the rule at the heart of AccessCast: the model proposes, code decides. An answer that breaks a rule is sent back, with the reason. Only an answer that passes every check reaches a viewer.
We attack it on purpose. We ask Gemma to simplify: press the button three times within ten seconds. On our site, anyone can run this live.

An answer that drops the ten seconds is blocked, and never reaches a viewer. In our recorded test, Gemma dropped it in {claim:e11.A5_number.production.gemma_failed} of {claim:e11.A5_number.production.tries} tries, and our checks blocked every one.
Or type your own caption, and watch it happen live.
In about half a minute, Gemma on AMD made the easy-read, Hindi and Italian versions. Our number check stopped one Italian line that turned 5 pm into 17:00, and the repair passed.

scenes.narration: Or give it any picture. Gemma, on AMD, lists what it sees and writes one line, and our rules check that line before anyone hears it.

On ten W3C accessibility videos we never tuned on, Gemma alone kept every not in {claim:e5.neg_gemma_k} of {claim:e5.neg_gemma_n} easy-read captions. What AccessCast published kept {claim:e5.neg_ours_k} of {claim:e5.neg_ours_n}.
Against specialist translation models, Gemma won on one of our two scores in all five languages. On the other score it lost for Hindi, French and Portuguese, and we report that.

Every Gemma call runs on AMD's Token Factory. From our own logs: {claim:amd.requests} requests and {claim:amd.tokens_millions} tokens, across {claim:amd.videos} videos. One finished minute of the five versions we measured costs about {claim:cost.usd_per_min} of Gemma, at list price.

The law already asks for this: in Europe since {claim:cited.law.eaa_apply_date}, in India since {claim:cited.law.india_mib_ott_date}, and for US public universities from {claim:cited.law.ada_title2_large_date}. They pay per finished minute, and their own staff approve every line.
AccessCast. Every viewer, the same video.
